These doctors are out of date.
LDL isn’t simply “bad” cholesterol. The picture is considerably more complicated than total LDL-C alone.
Examples from my experience with UK healthcare:
My GP wasn’t aware of the distinction between small, dense LDL and larger LDL particles, or of the evidence suggesting that LDL particle characteristics can influence cardiovascular risk.
Triglycerides and HDL can provide some information about metabolic health and LDL particle pattern, although they cannot by themselves tell you exactly what type of LDL you have.
My GP was also unaware of the BMJ study involving more than 68,000 people that reported an association between higher cholesterol and lower mortality among people over 60. That is an observational finding, so it doesn't by itself establish causation — but it certainly deserves discussion rather than simply saying “high cholesterol = bad”.
I’ve also had experiences with mainstream UK nutrition advice where basic points about nutrition were unclear. For example, an NHS nutritionist initially told me carrots contained vitamin A, when what they contain is beta-carotene, which the body can convert to retinol. They also weren’t aware that liver contains vitamin C.
I’ve also spoken to two NHS lipid specialists who stated that high cholesterol is “causal” in heart attacks. I think this needs much more nuance. Association alone cannot demonstrate causation, and the strength of evidence needs to be considered across different types of studies.
Likewise, studies showing that lowering LDL reduces cardiovascular events often involve populations with other major risk factors — such as type 2 diabetes, hypertension and obesity — so it is important to distinguish between different metabolic contexts rather than assuming everyone with a high LDL has the same underlying risk profile.
My concern is that some medical advice has become overly simplified:
“High LDL = disease. Lower LDL = better.”
The reality is more complicated. LDL particle number, ApoB, triglycerides, HDL, metabolic health, blood pressure, smoking, diabetes and other risk factors all matter when assessing cardiovascular risk.
Doctors and nutritionists should be willing to keep updating their advice as the evidence develops.

Nice video.
I was diagnosed with IBS at the age of 23, and my doctor told me to avoid eggs, milk, sugar, and (you guessed it) red meat. I also relied on what foods triggered my IBS symptoms, such as most veggies (cabbage, spinach, and more), beans, watermelons, etc.

As a 26-year-old tall guy from Cameroon living in Europe for 2 years now for a master's degree, I've moved between countries during my master's (the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, and Belgium). I decided to try carnivore when I was in Poland in July 2025, doing an internship, because of (you guessed it) Dr Tony Hampton and Dr Anthony Chaffee.

Personally, I realised fibre could be the problem, and too many carbs made me too hungry throughout the day. For someone who isn't always in one place at the same time, I end up eating whatever I can because I am hungry, but then end up triggering IBS symptoms.

So, in order to have the benefits of constant energy, avoid triggering IBS symptoms, and also avoid excessive weight gain, carnivore was the only lifestyle I could trust.


Today, I eat mostly low-budget carnivore meals on OMAD in the evening at around 4-5 pm-ish. Here are my recipes, keeping it as simple as possible.
1. 10 medium eggs with 1 sardine, fried in either pork lard, beef tallow or butter and salted to taste. Very satisfying. No hunger crashes during the day. No seasonings. This is my staple. Because it's the cheapest. 10 eggs cost, on average, 2.35 euros when on discount, and 1 sardine costs about 0.95 euros, depending on the brand and country. This is specifically for the Czech Republic. These are slightly more expensive in the Netherlands and Belgium

2. Meat. If I don't want eggs and sardines, I can eat about 600-700 grams of pork neck steak, salted to taste. No spicy seasonings.

3. Once or twice a week, I can have 1 kg of chicken (chicken thighs and drumsticks) boiled and then seared in pork lard. I season the chicken only with black and white pepper.

4. Once a week, I can also have a mixture of chicken heart, liver and gizzard for some rare nutrients. I fry it all in pork lard or butter.

5. Occasionally, I drink milk because it helps to fight cravings for fruit juices and carbonated beverages.

Hope you enjoyed this list, Dr Hampton. Thank you for your videos.
